scope: Only Śrīdhara's introductory passage under ŚB 10.1.1. Its eleven numbered introductory stanzas are NOT eleven Bhāgavatam verses. The rest of Chapter 1 remains unfinished word-for-word.

word_for_word: the universal creation, secondary creation and other [topics]
the tenth subject to be indicated
embodied as the support of those who depend upon him
in the ocean of the Yadu family
in the tenth canto, for the spreading of Kṛṣṇa's glorious renown
occasioned by the decline of dharma
beginning with the elemental or natural [dissolution]
through expositions of creation, destruction and related matters
to remove the burden of the earth
are spoken of in three divisions
in Greater Vṛndāvana and related places
difficult even for the gods [to perform]
in the waters of the Yamunā
her six children [in the womb / at birth]
delighted by the nectar of hearing the account of Kṛṣṇa's descent
through restating what was already said
[with the verse beginning] 'The expansion of the dynasties has been told'
entries.literal_english: Obeisance to Śrī Gaṇeśa. I bow to that supreme abode called Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the abode of the world, characterized by nine topics beginning with universal and secondary creation. In the tenth canto, the tenth subject is proclaimed as supreme bliss sporting in the ocean of the Yadu family, embodied as the support of those who depend on him. In order to spread Kṛṣṇa's true fame, the tenth canto describes the restraint of wicked rulers occasioned by the decline of dharma. Withdrawal, beginning with elemental dissolution, is explained in four divisions through accounts of creation, destruction, and related matters as each occasion arises. Ninety chapters in the tenth canto are composed for Kṛṣṇa's praise. In the first four, Hari's birth to relieve Earth's burden at Brahmā's request is related with its circumstances. Kṛṣṇa's pastimes are spoken of in three successive settings—Gokula, Mathurā, and Dvāravatī—and subdivided in many ways. Thirty-five chapters describe his pastimes while living in Gokula, including Greater Vṛndāvana, pastimes difficult even for the gods. One chapter gives Akrūra's hymn in the Yamunā's waters; eleven recount the pastimes in Madhuvana; the remainder describe Dvāravatī, including its construction. Thus the tenth canto has ninety chapters of detailed meaning. In the first, Kaṃsa, afraid after hearing that Devakī's son would cause his death, kills her six children. Delighted by the nectar of hearing Kṛṣṇa's descent, the king eagerly asks once more by restating what has already been narrated, beginning 'The expansion of the dynasties has been told.'
entries.editorial_note: The eleven internal numbered stanzas belong to Śrīdhara's introduction under Bhāgavatam 10.1.1. They are not Bhāgavatam verses 10.1.1–11. The source's typography merges the end of stanza 10 and beginning of stanza 11; they have been distinguished here without attributing any other commentator's words to Śrīdhara.
